title: Greetings and numbers 0–100
titleJp: あいさつと すうじ
canDo: I can greet people the right way for the time of day: おはようございます, こんにちは, こんばんは.
I can say goodbye and good night without mixing up さようなら, おやすみなさい and こんばんは.
I can thank someone, get someone's attention and apologize with ありがとうございます, どうも and すみません, and I can reply to a thank-you.
I can introduce myself for the first time with はじめまして。〜です。よろしく おねがいします。
I can say and understand any number from 0 to 100, including the double readings of 4, 7 and 9.

blocks.t: Warm-up: read this lesson's vocabulary (block 3) aloud, in kana only
Points 4a to 4c: greetings, thanks and self-introduction, with 🔊 and repetition
Points 4d and 4e: numbers from 0 to 100, counting aloud
Greetings and numbers video (block 6), pausing to repeat
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key

skills: Reading hiragana and katakana (lessons 00-1 and 00-2), even slowly: the names (マリア, ルーカス) and ゼロ are in katakana, and in the homework you write your own name in katakana.
Knowing what a long vowel is (lesson 00-1): おはよう, ありがとう, じゅう and きゅう depend on it.

grammar.title: Greetings for the time of day
grammar.gloss: good morning, hello, good evening, goodbye
grammar.explanation:
Japanese chooses a greeting by the **time of day** and by how **close** you are to the person. These are fixed formulas: learn each one as a single block.
• **おはようございます**: good morning, in the morning. With friends and family, just おはよう.
• **こんにちは**: hello, good afternoon — roughly from late morning to late afternoon. In general, it isn't used with your own family.
• **こんばんは**: good evening, **when arriving** or meeting someone in the evening.
• **おやすみなさい**: good night, **when going to bed** or parting late at night. With friends and family, おやすみ. The split works like English "good evening" (a hello) × "good night" (a goodbye).
• **さようなら**: goodbye. It can sound like a longer or more final farewell than English "bye"; among friends, day to day, じゃあね or また あした ("see you tomorrow") are more common. At school, though, it is the normal goodbye between students and their teacher.
• In こんにちは and こんばんは, the last は is read **wa**. It was originally the particle は, and the spelling stayed.
grammar.structure: morning: おはようございます · daytime: こんにちは · evening (arriving): こんばんは · bedtime: おやすみなさい · goodbye: さようなら

examples.jp: たなかせんせい、おはようございます。
examples.kana: たなかせんせい、おはようございます。

examples.jp: マリアさん、こんばんは。
examples.kana: マリアさん、こんばんは。
examples.en: Good evening, Maria. (meeting her in the evening)

examples.jp: おやすみなさい。— おやすみ。
examples.kana: おやすみなさい。— おやすみ。
examples.en: Good night. (a child going to bed) — Night! (the mother answers casually)

pitfalls: Using こんにちは as an all-purpose "hi" at any hour: in the morning it's おはようございます, and in the evening こんばんは.
Writing こんにちわ or こんばんわ ✗. The correct spelling uses は: こんにちは, こんばんは ✓.

Saying さようなら to friends you will see tomorrow: it can sound distant. Among friends, じゃあね or また あした. (At school, however, students usually say さようなら to the teacher at the end of the day; the workplace has other set phrases, which come later.)
Leaving off ございます with teachers and strangers: おはよう on its own is casual.
howToStudy: Speaking: tap 🔊 on each example and repeat it 3 times, holding the long vowel of おはよう (お・は・よ・う).
Throughout the day, quietly say the greeting for the time: when you wake up, おはようございます; in the afternoon, こんにちは; in the evening, こんばんは; before bed, おやすみなさい.
In your notebook, make a 2-column table (polite × casual) with this lesson's greetings.

grammar.title: すみません, どうも, ありがとう
grammar.explanation:
Three expressions you will use all the time, each with more than one job:
• **ありがとうございます**: thank you, polite. **ありがとう** alone is casual, for friends and family. To thank someone for something that is already over (at the end of a class, after someone has helped you), use ありがとうございました. It is also what the clerk says when you leave a shop.
• **どうも**: a short, very common "thanks" in daily life, for example when you get your change. Before ありがとうございます it adds emphasis: どうも ありがとうございます is "thank you very much".
• **すみません**: "excuse me", "I'm sorry" and sometimes "thank you (sorry for the trouble)". Use it to call a waiter, to squeeze past people, or to apologize for something small.
• To reply to a thank-you, the simplest answer is **いいえ** ("not at all"). どういたしまして ("you're welcome") also exists, but it sounds a bit stiff and textbook-like and is less common in everyday speech than you might expect. いいえ (or いえいえ) is the safe choice.
grammar.structure: thanks: ありがとうございます (casual: ありがとう) · excuse me / sorry: すみません · reply to a thank-you: いいえ

examples.jp: どうも ありがとうございます。— いいえ。
examples.kana: どうも ありがとうございます。— いいえ。
examples.en: Thank you very much. — Not at all.
Excuse me! (to call a waiter or to get past someone)

pitfalls: Using just ありがとう with a teacher or a stranger: it sounds too familiar. With them, ありがとうございます.
Thinking すみません only means "sorry". It is also the "excuse me" for getting someone's attention: calling out すみません！ in a restaurant is normal and polite.
Translating "you're welcome" as どういたしまして every time: it can sound stiff. A short いいえ (or いえいえ) is the everyday reply.
howToStudy: Speaking: act out pairs aloud. Say どうも ありがとうございます and answer いいえ; then say すみません！ as if calling a waiter.
Today, every time you say "thank you" in English, repeat ありがとうございます in your head.
In your notebook, write 3 situations from your own life (a shop, a class, a bus) and what you would say in Japanese in each one.

grammar.title: はじめまして・よろしく おねがいします
grammar.explanation:
To introduce yourself for the first time, Japanese uses a three-part formula, almost always in this order:
• **はじめまして。** "How do you do?" Literally something like "for the first time". It is only for a first meeting.
• **(name) です。** "I'm (name)." For now, use 〜です as a fixed block. In lesson 01-1 you will understand the full sentence (わたしは 〜です).
• **よろしく おねがいします。** It has no direct translation: roughly "please treat me kindly" or "I hope we get along". In an introduction, English "Nice to meet you" is the closest. It closes the introduction, usually with a slight bow (lesson 01-1).
• Among friends, just よろしく is fine. In a more formal situation, どうぞ よろしく おねがいします is more careful.
• よろしく おねがいします also shows up outside introductions — when asking a favor or when starting to work together: a general "I'm counting on you".
grammar.structure: はじめまして。 [name] です。 よろしく おねがいします。

examples.jp: はじめまして。ルーカスです。よろしく おねがいします。
examples.kana: はじめまして。ルーカスです。よろしく おねがいします。
examples.en: How do you do? I'm Lucas. Nice to meet you.

examples.jp: はじめまして。すずきです。どうぞ よろしく おねがいします。
examples.kana: はじめまして。すずきです。どうぞ よろしく おねがいします。
examples.romaji: Hajimemashite. Suzuki desu. Dōzo yoroshiku onegaishimasu.
examples.en: How do you do? I'm Suzuki. I'm very pleased to meet you. (more formal, with どうぞ)
I'm Ana. Nice to meet you! (casual, among classmates of the same age)

pitfalls: Using はじめまして with someone you have already met: it is only for the first meeting.
Putting さん on your own name: ルーカスさんです ✗ → ルーカスです ✓. さん is only for other people (lesson 01-1).
Translating よろしく おねがいします word by word. Treat it as a formula: it closes the introduction and shows goodwill.
Being surprised by family names: in formal situations, Japanese people usually introduce themselves by their family name (すずきです).
howToStudy: Speaking: record your full introduction (はじめまして。〜です。よろしく おねがいします。) and listen to it. Repeat until it comes out with no pauses.
In front of a mirror, do a slight bow on よろしく.
ヅオリンゴー → Journal: write your introduction and open "Anatomy of what I wrote": はじめまして and よろしく おねがいします show up as set phrases (INTERJECTION), and 〜です as the PREDICATE.

grammar.title: Numbers from 0 to 10
grammar.gloss: and the double readings of 4, 7 and 9
grammar.explanation:
The numbers from 0 to 10 are the base of everything: from 11 to 100, you just combine them.
• 0 ゼロ (also れい) · 1 いち · 2 に · 3 さん · 4 よん／し · 5 ご
• 6 ろく · 7 なな／しち · 8 はち · 9 きゅう／く · 10 じゅう
• **4, 7 and 9 have two readings.** For the number on its own and in the tens, prefer **よん, なな and きゅう**: they are the safest. し, しち and く appear in some counters and fixed words. For clock times (lesson 01-2), each number has its preferred reading.
• A common explanation is that し is avoided because it sounds the same as a word meaning "death", and く like one meaning "suffering".
• Watch the long vowels: じゅう (10) and きゅう (9) have う. Without it, じゅ and きゅ are not numbers.
• ろく uses the tapped r (like the "tt" in American "butter"), not an English r.
grammar.structure: 0 ゼロ · 1 いち · 2 に · 3 さん · 4 よん／し · 5 ご · 6 ろく · 7 なな／しち · 8 はち · 9 きゅう／く · 10 じゅう
pitfalls: Forgetting the long う: じゅ ✗ → じゅう ✓ (10), きゅ ✗ → きゅう ✓ (9).
Using し, しち and く in the tens: the standard forms are よんじゅう (40), ななじゅう (70) and きゅうじゅう (90).
Confusing し (4) and しち (7) in a fast list: one more reason to prefer よん and なな.
Reading ろく with an English r. It is the quick tap: "ro-ku".
howToStudy: Speaking: count from 0 to 10 and back, aloud, using よん, なな and きゅう.
ヅオリンゴー → Drills → Numbers: do one round and note which numbers made you stumble.
Say in Japanese the single-digit numbers you see during your day: the elevator floor, the bus line, the page of a book.

grammar.title: From 11 to 100
grammar.explanation:
From 11 to 99, Japanese is pure logic: say **how many tens**, then **じゅう**, then **the ones**. Unlike English, there are no special words like "eleven", "twelve" or "-teen": 11 is simply "ten-one".
• 11 = じゅう + いち → じゅういち · 15 = じゅうご · 19 = じゅうきゅう
• 20 = に + じゅう → にじゅう · 30 = さんじゅう · 40 = よんじゅう
• 34 = さん + じゅう + よん → さんじゅうよん · 87 = はちじゅうなな
• 10 is just じゅう, not いちじゅう. 100 is just **ひゃく**, not いちひゃく.
• Build it in the order you read the number: 56 → "5 tens and 6" → ごじゅうろく.
• In the ones place, よん, なな and きゅう are always safe, but you will also hear forms like じゅうしち (17).
grammar.structure: [tens] じゅう [ones] · 34 = さん・じゅう・よん · 100 = ひゃく
pitfalls: Saying いちじゅう for 10 or いちひゃく for 100 ✗: it is just じゅう and ひゃく ✓.
Reversing the order: 47 is よんじゅうなな (4-10-7). ななじゅうよん is 74.
Shortening じゅう in the middle of a number: にじゅ ✗ → にじゅう ✓ (20), with the long u.
howToStudy: Speaking: count by tens up to 100 (じゅう, にじゅう … ひゃく), and then by fives.
ヅオリンゴー → Drills → Numbers: another round, now paying attention to the tens.
Read aloud, in Japanese, the numbers up to 100 that you see during your day: a bus number, a book page, a price.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook, writing the Japanese in hiragana. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it in your next session.

tasks.prompt: Write in hiragana what you would say in each situation.

items.q: You arrive at your Japanese class at 9 a.m. and meet your teacher.
items.note: With a teacher, always with ございます.

items.q: At 3 p.m., you meet your Japanese neighbor in the elevator.
At 8 p.m., you arrive for dinner at a Japanese friend's house.
items.note: Arriving in the evening: こんばんは, not おやすみなさい.

items.q: You are staying with a Japanese family, and you are going to bed.
At a restaurant, you want to call the waiter.
A coworker lends you a pen. Thank them politely.

a.jp: ありがとうございます。

items.note: どうも ありがとうございます is great too. すみません ("sorry for the trouble") is also very natural here.

tasks.prompt: Write the numbers out in hiragana (0 goes in katakana).

items.note: You will also hear じゅうし.

tasks.prompt: Read aloud and write the number in digits.

items.note: しち is the other reading of 7.

tasks.prompt: Write your first self-introduction in 3 sentences: はじめまして, your name with です, and よろしく おねがいします. Then read it aloud and record it on your phone.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: はじめまして。ペドロです。よろしく おねがいします。
a.en: How do you do? I'm Pedro. Nice to meet you.

items.note: Check: your name in katakana and without さん, です right after the name, the full よろしく おねがいします, and 。 at the end of each sentence.

workbook.tip: Do it after points 4d and 4e. Check it with the official Genki Answer Key.

practice.what: Play normally. Whenever a greeting or a thank-you shows up in the dialogue (こんにちは, ありがとう, すみません…), pause, read it aloud and note in your notebook the situation in which the character used it.
Drills → Numbers: 2 rounds. If you still stumble on some letters, also do Kana → Free practice.
Tap 🔊 on each greeting and repeat along 3 times, keeping the long vowels (おはよう, ありがとう, さようなら).
Record your self-introduction (homework h4) in 15 seconds or less. Listen and check that はじめまして and よろしく おねがいします came out without pauses.
Count in Japanese whatever you come across: the stairs, your steps to the corner, the items on your shopping list. Go up to 100 when you can.

culture.title: Leaving home and coming back
culture.titleJp: いってきます／ただいま
culture.body: In Japan, leaving home and coming back have their own phrases, said almost every day. The person leaving says **いってきます** ("I'm off"; literally "I'll go and come back"), and the person staying answers **いってらっしゃい** ("see you later"; literally "go and come back"). The person arriving says **ただいま** ("I'm home"; literally "just now"), and whoever is at home answers **おかえりなさい** ("welcome back") or just **おかえり**, which is more casual. Some people say ただいま even when no one is home, out of pure habit. The same phrases are also often used at work, when leaving for an appointment and coming back.
culture.try: Adopt these phrases at home: say いってきます when you leave and ただいま when you arrive, even if no one answers. If you live with someone, teach them the replies: いってらっしゃい and おかえり.

checklist: I can choose the right greeting for morning, afternoon, evening and bedtime without looking.
I use ありがとうございます, どうも and すみません in the right situations and reply to a thank-you with いいえ.
I can give my full self-introduction (はじめまして … よろしく おねがいします) without pauses.
I can count from 0 to 100, and by tens, aloud and without stumbling.
I know both readings of 4, 7 and 9 and use よん, なな and きゅう in the tens.
I can write any number up to 100 in hiragana, with the long う of じゅう and きゅう.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
